Chapter 6: The Responsibilities of Church Leaders—Shepherding, Not Profiteering.
Now that we've talked about spiritual renewal and what genuine faith looks like, let’s turn our attention to something practical—what it really means to lead within the church community.
Here’s the thing: true leadership in the church isn’t about power, or chasing after wealth. It’s about serving, just like a shepherd cares for every single sheep, making sure they’re safe, healthy, and heading in the right direction.
So, what does this kind of leadership look like day to day?
First, genuine church leaders guide with humility. They put spiritual growth above their own interests, always thinking about what’s best for the people they serve. When it comes to offering advice or even gentle correction, they do it with kindness, aiming to lift others up—not tear them down.
Using church resources wisely is another huge responsibility. That means being open about where money goes, making sure it really supports those in need and furthers the church’s mission—not just padding the pockets or status of those in charge.
But what happens when leaders forget these responsibilities? Well, the church can quickly turn into an institution more interested in its own survival than actually serving its people. And honestly, when leaders use their spiritual authority for personal benefit, or to keep a tight grip on control, trust starts to fall apart. It’s even more damaging when spiritual promises get mixed up with things like selling indulgences or other financial schemes.
Think about a leader who’s more focused on keeping their title than really listening to the community. Over time, people start to feel ignored. The leader’s words lose their weight, and the whole atmosphere shifts. But flip that script—a leader who listens, who serves, who acts with humility? That’s the kind of person who builds trust and sparks real spiritual growth.
So, what’s the way forward? It’s all about recommitting to servant leadership. That means setting up ways to stay accountable, encouraging everyone to speak up, and truly listening to feedback from the whole community. Leaders also need to regularly check themselves—are their actions lining up with what Christ taught? Are they really meeting the needs of their people?
When church leaders embrace the role of shepherd instead of profiteer, something special happens. The church regains its integrity. Trust grows. Compassion spreads. And everyone starts working together with a sense of shared purpose.
